title: AI Can Bridge India's Public Healthcare Gaps, but Scaling Remains Hard
excerpt: At TechSparks 2026, Niramai, Wadhwani AI and Fundamentum experts said clinical validation, government integration and patient capital will decide whether AI screening reaches India's 150,000 primary health centres.
body:
• At TechSparks 2026, experts from Niramai, Wadhwani AI and Fundamentum said AI tools for early detection and frontline decision support will only work in India's public system if they are clinically validated in real settings, not just in laboratories.
  • India has around 150,000 primary health centres; Wadhwani AI has teams of five to seven people embedded in state health offices across 17 states to integrate tools into existing workflows.
  • Deployment is already at scale in government programmes: MadhuNetrAI has reviewed more than 14,000 retinal images for over 7,100 people in 38 centres across 11 states, and the Cough Against TB tool screened more than 162,000 people with case detection 12-16% higher than conventional methods.
  • For families in India and in the diaspora, the test is cost and access: Niramai aims to bring breast cancer screening below Rs 50 per person at scale, using a non-invasive thermal imaging process with no breast compression.

Startups are building artificial intelligence tools for remote monitoring, early disease detection and decision support for frontline health workers in India. The harder problem, a panel at TechSparks 2026 agreed, is integrating those tools into the public health system and making them work where connectivity is inconsistent, data are incomplete and care is delivered in many languages.

Dr Geetha Manjunath, founder and chief executive of Niramai Health Analytix, Debraj Banerjee of Fundamentum Frontier Advisors, and Shekar Sivasubramanian, head of Wadhwani AI, discussed why promising innovations often struggle to reach widespread adoption, according to YourStory's report of the panel. They identified three linked challenges: rigorous clinical validation, integration with public infrastructure, and the patient capital needed to scale.

"There are no gaps in the system. If you cannot solve a problem with these realities, then you shouldn't be in this business."

— Shekar Sivasubramanian, Head, Wadhwani AI

Validation in the field, not just the lab

Manjunath said the biggest barrier is the tendency to prioritise rapid product development over clinical validation. A model built in days from available datasets may perform well in a laboratory and fail on real patients, she said. Retrospective studies using hospital data with known outcomes are only a first step. Prospective studies test a technology live, without letting its predictions influence treatment, and compare the results with established clinical findings.

Even that is not enough for public deployment. A tool tested in a hospital must also be evaluated in rural settings where diagnostic infrastructure is limited, and its cost, feasibility and performance must all be considered before wider use. "The question is not whether you build your model. The real problem is to see if your algorithm actually works on real people," Manjunath said. "Healthcare requires more patience."

A MeitY-backed conclave in Varanasi on October 19 reached a similar conclusion, according to coverage of the conclave: prospective validation, data privacy, human-in-the-loop safeguards and low-bandwidth, multilingual design are non-negotiable.

What deployment looks like at government scale

Sivasubramanian said companies working in public health must understand the systems used by central and state governments. Wadhwani AI's embedded teams train users, map local requirements and adapt tools to existing workflows, because government officials implement the solutions and innovators act as facilitators.

That model is visible in national programmes. The Health Ministry has designated AIIMS Delhi, PGIMER Chandigarh and AIIMS Rishikesh as Centres of Excellence for AI, with Wadhwani AI support. MadhuNetrAI, which lets non-specialist workers screen for diabetic retinopathy, is live in 38 centres. AI integrated into eSanjeevani, the telemedicine platform, has supported more than 282 million consultations since April 2023.

Affordability as a design requirement

Manjunath cited Niramai's breast cancer screening as an example of designing for affordability, accessibility, acceptability and accuracy together. The tool uses thermal imaging and AI, without physical contact or breast compression, factors that discourage some women from screening. Niramai says it has screened around 700,000 women, aims for a cost below Rs 50 at scale, operates six centres in the United States using the solution, and has received US Food and Drug Administration approval for use alongside existing screening methods.

For investors, Banerjee said, the question is whether a company can navigate approvals, financing and distribution. Evaluators look for products that are segmented, nested within the relevant system and hyperlocalised, and venture capital is only one part of the ecosystem.

What this means for diaspora families

For Indian families abroad who rely on parents and relatives using primary health centres in India, the practical gain is earlier screening closer to home, rather than a referral chain to a distant specialist hospital. The next step to watch is whether validated tools move from pilots in a subset of states into routine use across the 150,000-centre network, with published field results, clear accountability for errors and pricing that public programmes can sustain.
